chunks: Quiescent current of a regulator. The question: What is quiescent current?
Quiescent current (Iq) is the small current a regulator draws just to stay alive, even with nothing connected to its output.
It runs the regulator's own circuits: a reference voltage to compare against, an amplifier that checks the output, and control logic. It is tiny, but it never switches off.
For a device that sleeps most of the time, Iq can be most of the energy used.
Think of a car idling at a red light. It is going nowhere, yet the engine still burns fuel every second. For a long trip the idling hardly matters.
For a car that sits waiting nearly all day, idling is nearly all the fuel. The regulator's Iq is the idling fuel.
The input current splits into two paths: I out flows through the pass element to the load, and the remaining I GND flows through the regulator's internal circuits to ground.
At no load, I GND equals I q .
Quiescent current (Iq): the current a regulator uses with no load. Ground current: the same current as seen leaving through the ground pin of an LDO.
Standby / sleep: a low-power state where the load draws very little. Load current: what the circuit actually draws from the output.
Light-load efficiency: efficiency when the load is small.
A coin cell holds 220 milliamp hours. A microcontroller sleeps at 2 microamps behind a regulator with an Iq of 50 microamps, so the total is 52 microamps.
The cell lasts about 220 over 0. 052 about 4200 hours, roughly 176 days.
With a 1 microamps part the total is 3 microamps, and the cell lasts about 73,000 hours, over 8 years in theory.
And if the load draws 10 microamps, a 50 microamps Iq means only 10 of every 60 microamps does useful work, so efficiency is below 17% (about 15% once the voltages are counted).
That is the whole idea.
"Quiescent current is what a regulator draws from its input just to operate, with no load: the bias for the reference, error amp, feedback divider and control.
For an LDO it's the ground-pin current.
It matters because it never goes away: in a battery device that sleeps at microamps, it can dominate standby current and light-load efficiency.
For example, 50 microamps on a coin cell kills standby life, so for always-on rails you pick nanoamp-class parts."
